# Theory

<!-- {{< include sections/lab1_theory.qmd >}} -->

## Why can it be important to consider various probability thresholds in the classification problems?

Different classifcation threshholds (r) affect trade-off between false
positives and false negatives. This can be particulary important when
the consequences of the different classification errors are not equally
severe. For example, lowering the threshold in disease detection can
identify more patients with the disease, but at the cost of more false
positives.

The preliminary 2026 pdf version of the book (Lindholm et al. 2022) shows example of this on page 92-93, example 4.5. It compares a default threshold of 0.5 with 0.15 for detecting thyroid
disease.

## What ways of collecting correct values of the target variable for the supervised learning problems are mentioned in the book?

From the preliminary 2026 pdf version of the book (Lindholm et al. 2022) we found several ways of obtaining the target values:

1.  Sometimes they are measured at the same time as inputs.

2.  Sometimes a domain expert label the data by hand e.g when a
    cardiologist assigns a diagnosis to each ECG signal (p.16)

3.  They can come from automated computations, such as the density
    functional theory simulations in the materials example.

4.  They can come from historical records like past match results (p.6)

5.  In self-supervised learning the targets are derived from the data
    itself, e.g by predicting the next value in a time series (p.38-39)

## How can one express the cost function of the linear regression in the matrix form, according to the book?

The cost function for linear regression with squared error loss can be
expressed in matrix form as,

$$
J(\boldsymbol{\theta})
= \frac{1}{n}\|X\boldsymbol{\theta}-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2,
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is the vector of
regression coefficients, $\mathbf{y}$ is the vector of observed
responses, and $n$ is the number of observations. The cost function
represents the mean squared error between the predicted and observed
values and is minimized when estimating the regression coefficients.

The preliminary 2026 pdf version of the book (Lindholm et al. 2022) shows this on page 45, equation (3.11)
